'''Edward Raymond Andrew''' (27 June 1921 &ndash; 27 May 2001) was a 20th-century British scientist who was a pioneer of [[nuclear magnetic resonance]]. He was a primary figure in the development and creation of the world's first [[MRI scanner]].

==Life==
He was born in [[Boston, Lincolnshire]], on 27 June 1921 the only child of English parents of Scots descent. He was educated at [[Wellingborough School]] where he was head boy. He then won a place at [[Christ's College, Cambridge]] on a Natural Science Tripos from 1939 to 1942 under [[C. P. Snow]], [[Lawrence Bragg]], [[Norman Feather]], and [[David Shoenberg]].<ref>Independent (newspaper) obituary 26 July 2001</ref>

From 1942 to 1945, during the [[Second World War]], he was a Scientific Officer at the Air Defence Research and Development Establishment in [[Malvern, Worcestershire|Malvern]] studying the effects of gun flashes on [[radar]].<ref name="RSE">{{cite web |url=http://www.rse.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/andrew_edward.pdf |title=Edward Raymond Andrew |vauthors = Turnstall D |date= |website= |publisher= |access-date=March 14, 2020}}</ref>

In 1945 he returned to Cambridge as a research student at [[Pembroke College, Cambridge|Pembroke College]] and the [[Cavendish Laboratory]]. Here he worked with David Shoenberg on [[superconductors]], gaining a doctorate (PhD) in 1948. He then went to [[Harvard University]] for a year to work on [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] with [[Edward Mills Purcell|Ed Purcell]] and Bersohn, also working on the [[Pake doublet]].<ref name="RSE"/>

He returned to Britain in 1949 to work with [[John F. Allen (physicist)|Jack Allen]] FRS at the Cavendish. Colleagues on the NMR project included [[Bob Eades]], [[Dan Hyndman]], and [[Alwyn Rushworth]].<ref name="RSE" /> His students here included [[Waldo Hinshaw]].

In March 1952, he was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]].<ref name="RSE"/>

In 1954, he became a professor and head of physics at the [[University of North Wales]] in Bangor.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bottomley |first=Paul A. |last2=Mansfield |first2=Peter |last3=Allen |first3=Peter S. |date=2001 |title=E. Raymond Andrew. June 27, 1921–May 27, 2001 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/mrm.1207 |journal=Magnetic Resonance in Medicine |language=en |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=417–418 |doi=10.1002/mrm.1207 |issn=1522-2594 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sheppard |first=Norman |date=2003-01-01 |title=Edward Raymond Andrew. 27 June 1921 – 27 May 2001 |url=https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbm.2003.0001 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |issue=49 |pages=1–14 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2003.0001 |issn=0080-4606 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Here he founded the British Radio-Frequency Spectroscopy Group (BRSG).

In 1964, he moved to a chair at the [[University of Nottingham]] in place of Prof [[L. F. Bates]]. His work here included the development of the [[MRI scanner]] from 1975 to 1977. In 1978, their success led to the development of the whole-body MRI scanner.{{dubious|date=January 2021}}

After 19 years in Nottingham, he moved to the [[University of Florida]] in [[Gainesville, Florida|Gainesville]] as a Graduate Professor of Radiology, Physics, and Nuclear Engineering.

In 1984, he was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of London]],<ref name="RSE" /> and won their [[Wellcome Medal]] in the same year.

He died on 27 May 2001, aged 79.

==Family==

He was married twice: firstly to Mary with whom he had two daughters (Patricia and Charmian); and secondly in 1972 to Eunice.

==Publications==

*''Magnetic Resonance in Medicine'' (1984)
